newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa stable, doctors act on heart rhythm.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa stable, doctors act on heart rhythm.

text.p: Mother Teresa's condition was stable on Sunday and doctors said they were trying to correct an irregular heart rhythm following life-saving surgery.
"She is stable. She had a good sleep last night. She is comfortable and cheerful," said a medical bulletin issued by the B.M. Birla Heart Research Centre in the Indian city of Calcutta.
The 86-year-old Roman Catholic nun had surgery on Friday to clear two coronary artery blockages, which one doctor said would have led to a fatal heart attack if untreated.
Mother Teresa, the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner and known as the "Saint of the Gutters" for her devotion to the poor, destitute and dying, was fitted with a heart pacemaker in 1989.
Patricia Aubanel, an American doctor on her medical panel, said on Saturday that Mother Teresa had developed signs of bronchial pneumonia, which was being treated.
Dr D.P. Shetty, the panel leader, told reporters on Sunday doctors had started using drugs to try to correct her arhythmia, or irregular heart rhythm.
"We are trying to correct her arhythmia with medicine and we will watch her for two or three days.
"If it does not work, then only we have to go for mild electric shock or the mechanical cardioversion," he added.
Aubanel, who treated Mother Teresa in California in 1991, said cardioversion treatment for an arhythmia was essential.
"It is absolutely necessary now for her to go for the cardioversion... There is some risk but she can't leave the hospital without this treatment," she said.
"Our first choice is pharmacological cardioversion because Mother Teresa had refused to have electric shocks on a couple of occasions before," Aubanel added.
Aubanel also said: "She has some sign of bronchial pneumonia and we are treating that as her lung congestion is still persisting."
Doctors have stressed that Mother Teresa, who on Saturday told a senior clinic official she felt fine and was ready to go home, was not yet out of danger.
Nuns at the Calcutta headquarters of Mother Teresa's Missionaries of Charity order said its members worldwide were praying for her recovery.
The Roman Catholic order, with about 4,500 nuns in 111 countries, was founded by Mother Teresa in 1949.
After Friday's surgery, Aubanel said angioplasty had saved Mother Teresa's life.
She said some danger remained to Mother Teresa's heart and it would take her up to three months to recover.
"She was going to have a heart attack -- a major heart attack -- if the angioplasty was not done. Mother could not have left the hospital alive without this angioplasty," Aubanel said.
Angiography is an X-ray test which uses an injected opaque dye to show up blocked arteries. Angioplasty is the procedure to unblock the artery by inserting a balloon and inflating it.
The procedures, the third time she had undergone them in five years, were performed eight days after Mother Teresa entered hospital with an irregular heartbeat.
Doctors said Mother Teresa, born of Albanian parents as Gonxhe Bojaxhi, had suffered heart failure several times since entering the Woodlands Nursing Home in Calcutta on November 22.
She was moved to the Birla clinic last Tuesday.
